title: How are you using AI to make... your AI?
author: YuukiCrypto
selftext:
Before AI became synonymous with transformers (GPT), AI used to be mainly to reference the enemy systems in your game. So I am curious, how are you all using AI to build AI? 

It seems like one of the most powerful pieces of a game, having AI that *feels* good. I have not been able to explore it much, but after sharing a clip of my current combat - I realized I needed to show the enemies in my game a lot more love.

The one thing I found to be harsh when designing intelligent AI systems for your NPC is that the more you add to the game, the more your AI has to know. I had to step back and look at some of the industry standards to see how it has been managed by other dev teams.

[GameAI Pro ](https://www.gameaipro.com/GameAIPro/GameAIPro_Chapter10_Building_Utility_Decisions_into_Your_Existing_Behavior_Tree.pdf)has tons of great design documents on how this should work in your games. Have you been using anything other than behavior trees in your game?

comments.body: I'm using a weighted prediction system at the moment. It has lots of bugs but works well enough. comments.author: FridgeBaron
comments.body:
Depending on your game it's fairly trivial to have the AI make an AI benchmarking system. You are obviously going to be responsible for how it all feels at the end of the day but data is a super valuable weapon.

My current system uses a behaviour tree and I track almost everything. I can pit bots vs bots over and over mutating them and picking which one I want to fight for myself to feel what ones feel better.

Balance is a big part of feel so having an enemy with to high accuracy or that is doing way more damage is also things a tracker will give you incite on fixing. Hell even just playing a bunch and rating the round can be a way to find your weakest spots.

comments.author: Heath_co
comments.body:
For using NPC neural networks I build the game in a way that NPC AI can read information with a fixed set of numbers. And then train them with self play like a chess AI or alpha Go

I am making a mario kart style game where npc's will navigate along a track.

The track is built with curves that have a width and upwards orientation. Features (like boost pads and item boxes) are placed on the track as points on the curve, with a distance from the centre.

NPC's can see a distance down the track, its features, and enemy kart positions and speeds. All of these things can be represented with numbers, meaning NPC neural networks can see them. They can also see the stats of their own kart.

The NPC neural nets then output numbers which represents its controller inputs, and do this every game tick.

The AI's will be trained to different proficiencies to represent different difficulty levels.

The downsides to this is it constrains the amount of features I can use, and implementing a new feature involves training up a new AI.

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body:
A combination of JEV and deterministic, emergent oracle systems that provide it options to choose from. Don't want to go into more detail than that.

General combat behaviours are still governed by classic AI profiles (coward, berserker, protector, etc) and weights to certain actions. Targeting is perfect though has random modifiers depending on the character for things like delayed actions or target shifts in order to portray realistic accuracy or decision making. Would be too easy to make a perfect combat AI that just obliterated any human without adding some failure-rates.

In regards to the AI-needing-to-know-things comment... You can modularize the AI so that certain packages are only active if the player has certain weapons, abilities or whatever equipped. I mean you still have to create and program these behaviour libraries, but in terms of activity and performance, proper triggering is of course the best way to handle them as opposed to everything being loaded into one single giant AI package.

comments.author: AkandoGames
comments.body:
Mine’s an autobattler, so the AI works a bit differently. I use a custom priority-rule system: fighters read ordered IF/THEN commands for attacking, defending, moving and choosing targets. Custom state machines handle the execution, tracking things like attack phases, dodges, cooldowns and weapon switching.

Players and opponents use the same combat rules and tactic system. Players write their own tactics, while opponents get prebuilt sets based on their role, equipment and how sophisticated the campaign expects them to be ..

comments.author: johnesco
comments.body:
I was making a car racing game, but I wanted the car to "drive itself" on the demo screen and Claude made a simple bot. Then that turned into other traffic in the game. Then I gave them motivations (this was all in prompts) to make them drive an take risks and cautions, then I gave them memory for grudges and retaliation. It's not quite like boids or flocking, but generally they aim for points ahead and steer around (or into traffic). This naturally limits what it can see and react to, to cap calculations needed.

I've always called that AI, but in the time of LLM, how do we say "coded deterministic ai"? What do we call the OLD ai as to not confuse it with the new? Or do we make sure to say LLM AI when we talk about those the new?
